short: According to Noelle-Neumann, an almost statistician-like “sixth sense” that lets people, without running a poll, sense which opinion is rising and which is declining around them.
body:
The quasi-statistical sense (the sources also use *quasi-statistical organ*) is a concept Noelle-Neumann proposed to describe how people sense the distribution of opinion around them. The idea: alongside the five senses there is a kind of sixth sense, and this sense collects what society at large thinks and what is in favour “almost statistically”, without a random sample or a poll. [[cite:griffin-2009]][[cite:polat-2016]]

According to Noelle-Neumann, this perception catches especially the *direction of travel*, that is, which opinion is rising and which is declining; even when people misread the present state, they generally sense the trend. [[cite:griffin-2009]] That is why two questions are asked in her research: “Whatever your own opinion, what do most people think?” and “In a year’s time, will more or fewer people share this opinion?” [[cite:griffin-2009]]

Turkish has no established equivalent. The Turkish version of this course uses “yarı istatistiksel algı” (“quasi-statistical perception”), as does one Turkish article [[cite:kehya-2018]]; Polat’s text conveys the concept by explaining it as “neredeyse istatistiki bir anlayış gücü” (“an almost statistical power of understanding”). [[cite:polat-2016]]
example: In 1965, while voting intentions stayed steady for months, answers to “Who do you think will win the election?” shifted toward the CDU/CSU: even though the parties’ real strength had not changed, people had sensed which way the trend was turning. [[cite:polat-2016]][[cite:petersen-2019]]
